subject: DBMS
questions: A DBMS is software that stores, retrieves and manages data in databases.
Which is an advantage of a DBMS over plain files?
Controlled concurrent access and less redundancy
A DBMS reduces redundancy and manages concurrency, integrity and security.
The data stored at a moment
The overall design/structure of the database
The schema describes structure; an instance is the data at a point in time.
The three-level ANSI/SPARC architecture has which levels?
Changing physical storage without changing the logical schema
Changing the logical schema without changing external views/applications
Physical independence is about storage; logical independence is about the conceptual schema.
Data about data, such as table definitions
Which language defines tables and their structure?
Data Definition Language: CREATE, ALTER, DROP.
Data Manipulation Language works with the rows.
Who is responsible for managing a database's security, backups and performance?
The DBA administers the database system.
In an ER diagram, what does a rectangle represent?
Rectangles are entity sets; ellipses are attributes; diamonds are relationships.
What does a diamond represent in an ER diagram?
An entity that cannot be identified by its own attributes alone
A weak entity depends on an owner entity and has a partial key.
A multivalued attribute is drawn as ...
Double ellipses show multivalued attributes such as phone numbers.
A derived attribute (like age from date of birth) is drawn as ...
One student enrols in many courses and one course has many students. This cardinality is ...
Both sides can have many: M:N.
How is an M:N relationship usually mapped to tables?
Create a separate table with both primary keys as foreign keys
Add a column to one table
A junction (associative) table holds pairs of keys.
Double lines mean every entity must take part in the relationship.
What is generalisation in the EER model?
Combining similar entities into a higher-level entity
Generalisation is bottom-up; specialisation is top-down.
A composite attribute is one that ...
Can be divided into smaller parts, like a full address
Address can be split into street, city, PIN code.
In the relational model, a row is also called a ...
Rows are tuples; columns are attributes.
A chosen candidate key that uniquely identifies each row
It must be unique and not null.
A key that is unique in its own table
An attribute that refers to a primary key in another (or the same) table
A key with null values only
A candidate key is a superkey with no unnecessary attributes.
Any set of attributes that uniquely identifies rows
Superkeys may contain extra attributes; candidate keys are minimal ones.
The primary key cannot be null
No part of a primary key may be NULL.
Every foreign key value matches an existing primary key value (or is null)
It prevents references to rows that do not exist.
The degree of a relation is its number of ...
The cardinality of a relation is its number of ...
A key made of two or more columns
For example (student_id, course_id) in an enrolment table.
Which clause filters rows before grouping?
WHERE filters rows; HAVING filters groups.
Which clause filters groups after GROUP BY?
HAVING can use aggregates such as COUNT(*) > 5.
Removes duplicate rows from the result
DISTINCT returns each different row once.
Which is the correct pattern to find names starting with 'A'?
The number of non-null values in a column
COUNT(*) counts rows, including those with nulls.
How do you test for a missing value in SQL?
Comparisons with NULL are unknown; use IS NULL.
UPDATE table SET col = value WHERE ...
What is the difference between DELETE and TRUNCATE?
TRUNCATE removes all rows quickly (usually without row-by-row logging); DELETE can use WHERE
DELETE is DML and can filter rows; TRUNCATE empties the table.
Which query returns the second highest salary?
SELECT MAX(salary) FROM emp WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM emp)
Take the maximum among salaries below the overall maximum.
Which join returns only rows with matches in both tables?
INNER JOIN keeps matching pairs only.
All rows of the left table, with NULLs where the right has no match
All rows of the right table
Unmatched left rows appear with NULLs for right columns.
A CROSS JOIN of tables with 3 and 4 rows produces how many rows?
It is the Cartesian product: 3 x 4.
A join on primary keys only
Used for hierarchies such as employee-manager in one table.
A subquery that refers to columns of the outer query
It is evaluated for each row of the outer query.
Which operator checks whether a subquery returns any rows?
EXISTS is true if the subquery returns at least one row.
Combines rows of two queries and removes duplicates
A natural join joins tables on ...
All columns with the same name
Natural join matches columns sharing names and keeps one copy.
All rows from both tables, matched where possible
Nothing if any row is unmatched
Unmatched rows from either side appear with NULLs.
A physical copy of a table
A stored query that behaves like a virtual table
Views simplify queries and can restrict access.
What is the main goal of normalization?
Normalization organises tables to avoid anomalies.
It has a primary key only
All attribute values are atomic (no repeating groups)
Each cell holds a single value.
Partial dependencies on part of a composite key
Non-key attributes must depend on the whole key.
Non-key attributes must not depend on other non-key attributes.
A relation is in BCNF if for every non-trivial FD X -> Y ...
What is a functional dependency X -> Y?
Each value of X determines exactly one value of Y
Rows that agree on X must agree on Y.
Which anomaly happens when deleting a row loses other facts?
Example: deleting the last student of a course removes the course's details.
Deliberately adding redundancy to speed up reads
It trades update cost for read performance.
Joining the parts gives back exactly the original relation
No spurious tuples appear after the join.
These are the four properties of reliable transactions.
All of a transaction's operations happen, or none do
A failed transaction is rolled back completely.
Logs and storage make committed results permanent.
Which command makes a transaction's changes permanent?
Which command undoes the current transaction's changes?
ROLLBACK returns to the state before the transaction (or a savepoint).
Each transaction appears to run alone, unaffected by others' partial work
Concurrent transactions should not see each other's uncommitted changes.
Reading data written by a transaction that has not committed
If that transaction rolls back, the read value never existed.
It is conflict-equivalent to some serial schedule
Checked with an acyclic precedence graph.
A backup of the whole database
A marker inside a transaction you can roll back to
ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT undoes work after the marker only.
Which isolation level prevents dirty, non-repeatable and phantom reads?
SERIALIZABLE is the strictest standard level.
A growing phase of acquiring locks, then a shrinking phase of releasing them
Once a transaction releases a lock it may not acquire new ones; this ensures serializability.
Two or more transactions each waiting for locks the others hold
Reading by several transactions at once
Many S locks can coexist; an X lock is exclusive.
Which is a way to handle deadlocks?
Detect with a wait-for graph and abort a victim
Prevention (e.g. wait-die), avoidance or detection plus recovery.
In the wait-die scheme, an older transaction requesting a lock held by a younger one ...
Older waits for younger; a younger requester dies (is rolled back).
Data is written before the log
Log records are written to stable storage before the data pages they describe
WAL makes undo and redo possible after a crash.
What is a checkpoint used for in recovery?
Limiting how much of the log must be scanned after a crash
At a checkpoint, dirty pages are flushed and a marker is logged.
After a crash, committed transactions whose changes were not on disk must be ...
Redo committed work; undo uncommitted work.
Timestamp ordering protocol orders conflicting operations by ...
Operations violating timestamp order cause a rollback.
The lost update problem happens when ...
Two transactions overwrite each other's update without seeing it
Proper locking or isolation prevents it.
What is the main purpose of an index?
Indexes avoid full table scans at the cost of extra writes and storage.
Which structure do most databases use for indexes?
B+ trees keep data sorted with fast range scans.
In a B+ tree, where are the actual data pointers stored?
Leaves hold the keys with record pointers and are linked for range scans.
The order rows are physically stored
A table can have only one clustered index.
Hashing does not keep order, so ranges are slow.
What is a disadvantage of many indexes?
Every index must be updated when data changes.
An entry for every search key value
A sparse index has entries for only some values (e.g. one per block).
Mirroring (a full copy on another disk)
RAID 0 stripes; RAID 1 mirrors; RAID 5 uses distributed parity.
Which kind of database stores data as documents, such as JSON?
Document databases store flexible, nested records.
The CAP theorem says a distributed system cannot fully guarantee all of ...
During a network partition you trade consistency against availability.
A named set of SQL statements stored in the database and run on request
Procedures can take parameters and contain logic.
SQL code that runs automatically on events such as INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE
Triggers enforce rules or keep audit logs.
Before the new row is inserted, and can change or reject it
AFTER triggers run once the change is made.
What is a cursor in SQL?
A way to process query results one row at a time
Cursors are used in procedural SQL such as PL/SQL.
It adds variables, loops and exceptions to SQL.
An advantage of stored procedures is ...
Less network traffic and logic kept close to the data
Many statements run in one call on the server.
In a row-level trigger, which keywords refer to the old and new values?
For example :NEW.salary in Oracle or NEW.salary in MySQL.
What is a function in SQL compared with a procedure?
A function returns a value and can be used in queries
Procedures are called with CALL/EXEC and need not return a value.
Hidden automatic logic can make behaviour hard to follow and slow down writes
